name: Hana Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run pick-and-place machines at an electronics plant on the business park. They're machines that put tiny parts, smaller than a grain of rice, onto circuit boards for things like heating controls and car chargers. I load the reels of parts onto the feeders, start each batch, watch the camera checks and deal with errors, and when a feeder jams I'm still calling Priya, the technician, more than I'd like. It's clean and quiet compared to most factories, but you stare at screens and tiny things all day, and my eyes are done by home time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the plant?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ten months ago. I was a hairdresser for eighteen years, renting a chair in a salon, until the owner retired and sold the building for flats. I still cut hair in my kitchen on Saturdays for cash. My partner Mark is a shift supervisor at a warehouse, our daughter Ruby is thirteen and Sam is ten, and with the mortgage we're always about three weeks from trouble. I use AI for everything, honestly: our budget, Sam's spelling tests, and asking what the feeder error codes mean before Priya gets there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? Mostly hype? I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest. I've found it so useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a handy tool, it just didn't take over the world. People who were scared can relax, and people like me keep using it. I'd probably post something like "told you it was just a clever helper".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fine for me. I'd keep using it to learn faster, and maybe in a year or two I could move up to setting the machines instead of just running them. That's real money for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep studying the machines with the chatbot in my breaks, ask Priya if I can shadow her on changeovers, keep the Saturday haircuts going. Maybe try to save the haircut money instead of spending it on the kids' shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be a bit disappointed. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like that it lets someone like me catch up. I left school at sixteen. Now I can ask it what a capacitor is at eleven at night and not feel stupid. If it stays a small thing, that's fine, but I'd like it to get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Priya think of you using it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She laughs at me, but she's started asking me to look things up for her too. Last month it told me the wrong part number once, so I always check now. You learn to trust it like a new apprentice, not like a boss.

S0.say: It's still a handy tool; it just didn't take over the world. People who were scared can relax, and people like me will keep using it.
S0.think: It's fine for me, because I'll keep using it to learn faster. In a year or two I could move up to setting the machines, and that's real money for us.
S0.do: Keeps studying the machines with the chatbot on breaks and asks to shadow the technician on changeovers. Keeps the Saturday haircuts going and tries to save that money.
S0.quote: You learn to trust it like a new apprentice, not like a boss.
S0.fieldNote: Hana says plainly she would be disappointed if AI stayed small, because it helps her catch up after leaving school at sixteen. She's sensible about its mistakes and checks its answers. The Saturday haircuts are already a small second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one I think I could work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming either way, so you might as well be on the front foot. Learn the new tools, ask for training, don't wait to be told. I'd say people shouldn't expect the company or the government to sort it all out, but they should help a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a decent spot for this one, even though I'm junior. The other operators mostly avoid the screens. If the machines get smarter, someone has to set them up and talk to them, and I'm already the one doing that at night with my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager straight away about the technician course the company sends people on, and offer to do it partly in my own time. I'd keep learning with the chatbot every day. If they wouldn't pay, I'd find an online course and do it in the evenings, I've done harder things with two kids. I'd keep the haircuts as backup money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit excited. Nervous about money, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do a course in your own time with two kids. When, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After nine, when Sam's asleep and Ruby's on her phone pretending to be asleep. Mark does the dishes. It's what I did when I was learning to do colours at the salon, years ago, with Ruby as a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, on the line next to me. He's been there twenty years and he won't even use the tablet for the shift log, he writes it on paper and someone types it up. He's kind, he showed me everything when I started. I'd try to drag him along with me, but I don't think he'd come.

S1.say: Change is coming either way, so you might as well be on the front foot. Learn the tools and ask for training; don't expect the company or the government to sort it all out, though they should help a bit.
S1.think: I think I'm in a decent spot even though I'm junior, because the other operators avoid the screens. If the machines get smarter, someone has to set them up, and I'm already doing that at night on my phone.
S1.do: Asks the manager right away about the company technician course and offers some of her own time. Keeps learning daily with AI, finds an online course if the company won't pay, and keeps haircuts as backup money.
S1.feel: A bit excited, with some nerves about money.
S1.quote: After nine, when Sam's asleep and Ruby's on her phone pretending to be asleep.
S1.fieldNote: Hana sees the steady disruption picture as a chance, despite thin savings and being junior. Her self-reliance is pragmatic rather than ideological: she wants some help but won't wait for it. She has a track record of learning at night with small kids, which makes the plan believable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's different. Even the technician job goes, doesn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready and we'll all need to be flexible, and that the government needs to do something fast to stop people losing their homes. I wouldn't say I know the answer, because I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my head start with the tools doesn't help if the tools can do the job without me. What I've got is my hands and people who like me cutting their hair. That's honestly what I'd fall back on. Whether people still want a human haircut when a robot can do it, I don't know, but I think some would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd build up the haircuts, put up a sign at the school and the corner shop, maybe do home visits for older people who can't get out. We'd cut back hard, the kids' activities, the car payments if we can sell and buy cheaper. I'd use AI to find whatever work is going and to sort out the money. I'd keep the factory job until they let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. But I'd be too busy to sit with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Home visits for older people: why there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my nan had a lady come to do her hair every two weeks, and it was the best day of her fortnight. It's not the haircut, it's the chat. I don't think people want to tell a robot about their grandson's wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could the haircuts bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now it's maybe a hundred and fifty a month. If I really pushed it, evenings and weekends, maybe six or seven hundred. That's not the mortgage, but it's food and the bills.

S2.say: Nobody's ready and we'll all need to be flexible. The government needs to act fast to stop people losing their homes, and I don't pretend to know the answer.
S2.think: My head start with the tools doesn't help if they can do the job without me. What I've got is my hands and people who like me cutting their hair, and I think some would still want a human.
S2.do: Builds up the haircuts with signs at the school and corner shop and home visits for older people. Cuts kids' activities and swaps to a cheaper car, uses AI to find work and manage money, and keeps the factory job until she's let go.
S2.feel: Scared, but too busy to sit with it.
S2.quote: I don't think people want to tell a robot about their grandson's wedding.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI makes Hana's tech head start feel worthless, and she falls back on her older trade: hair and conversation. She has rough numbers ready, which shows how she thinks. She stays active even when scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it. Enough to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so use it. Learn what you can, build something on the side, and the government should make sure people don't fall through the cracks while it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do two things at once: get onto the technician course for the next few years of money, and slowly build a little mobile hairdressing business for after. One pays now, one's for later. That's how I'd see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year: the technician course, mostly paid by the company if I can push them. Use the chatbot to study and to set up a simple booking page for the haircuts. Put every bit of technician pay rise into savings. Get proper insurance so I can do home visits legally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but busy and hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one pays now and one's for later. Doesn't that leave you exhausted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. Mark says I'm already running on fumes. But five years of tired is better than two years of panic. And the kids are getting older, Ruby could help with the booking stuff, she'd love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the factory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until the hair business is paying more than half the bills. I'm not daft. Maybe year four. I'd want a cushion first, which we've never had.

S3.say: We've got time, so use it: learn what you can and build something on the side. The government should make sure people don't fall through the cracks while it happens.
S3.think: I'd do two things at once: the technician course for the next few years of money, and slowly building a mobile hairdressing business for later. One pays now, one's for after.
S3.do: Takes the technician course in the first year, pushing the company to pay, and uses AI to study and set up a booking page. Saves every pay rise and gets insurance for home visits.
S3.quote: But five years of tired is better than two years of panic.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Hana runs a two-track plan, one for now and one for later. She's clear she won't leave the factory until the side business covers half the bills. Mark's "running on fumes" is a hint of the cost of all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be fifty-three. Ruby would be twenty-three. That's a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to try. Start now, small steps. I'd also say the government should make sure older people and people who struggle with tech aren't left behind, because not everyone's like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I feel okay about this one. Ten years is enough to get the technician job, earn better for a while, and build the hair business properly. The end point is the same, but I'd be close to the end of my working life, with something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the course next year, then save for a proper portable kit and maybe a small van in year three or four. I'd use AI for the bookings, the accounts, the marketing. I'd tell Ruby and Sam to learn the tools but also learn something with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A little uneasy about the end, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "not everyone's like me". Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, and my mum. She can't do online banking. If everything goes digital and robotic, she's lost. I can help her, but not everyone has a daughter who can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is buying a van a risk, with savings as thin as yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a risk, yes. But ten years of planning, I'd only buy it when the haircuts already pay for it. I'd rather take a careful risk than sit and wait for the robot.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for anyone willing to try, so start now with small steps. The government should make sure older people and those who struggle with tech aren't left behind.
S4.think: I feel okay about this one, because ten years is enough to get the technician job and build the hair business properly. The end point is the same, but I'd be near the end of my working life with something of my own.
S4.do: Starts the technician course next year and saves for a portable kit and a small van by year three or four. Uses AI for bookings, accounts and marketing, and advises her children to learn both tools and a hands-on skill.
S4.feel: Mostly hopeful, slightly uneasy about the end.
S4.quote: I'd rather take a careful risk than sit and wait for the robot.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Hana build a business of her own, funded only once it pays for itself. She thinks about people less able to adapt, like her mother and Gary. Her calm comes from her skills and plans, not from savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My tech head start doesn't mean much if there's no time. What would help is a bit of breathing room on the mortgage, and making it easy to start a small business, without a mountain of forms and fees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people did before the factory. Half of us had another life, a trade or a shop. That's where some of us would go back to.

headlineQuote: Half of us had another life, a trade or a shop. That's where some of us would go back to.
portrait: Hana is forty-three, a former hairdresser who started running pick-and-place machines at an electronics plant ten months ago, after her salon was sold. She uses AI every day, for work, budgeting and her kids' homework, and treats it like an apprentice she checks. In the slower scenarios she'd move fast into technician training while building a mobile hairdressing business on the side. With two years, she falls back on her hands and her clients, and she worries about people like her mum and her colleague Gary who can't adapt as easily.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her tech head start means little without time, and the family has only about three weeks of money.
whatWouldHelp: Breathing room on the mortgage, and making it easy to start a small business without lots of forms and fees.
